originalTitle: Espionage, true crime and war: Baillie Gifford longlist revealed
summary: Patrick Radden Keefe, Ben Macintyre and the Guardian’s Charlotte Higgins are among the 13 authors selected for the nonfiction award
content: The Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins joins American investigative journalist Patrick Radden Keefe and bestselling historian Ben Macintyre on this year’s Baillie Gifford prize longlist. Higgins’ book, Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War, examines the role of culture in Ukraine’s resistance to Russia’s invasion, drawing on multiple reporting trips to Ukraine. Keefe, who won the prize in 2021 with Empire of Pain, is listed again for London Falling, which tells the story of Zac Brettler, a teenager who fell from a luxury London apartment after having posed as the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch. Macintyre’s Redwood: The Untold Story of the Cold War’s Most Extraordinary Spy, tells the story of a KGB double agent cultivated by MI6 in revolutionary Tehran. The 13 books on the longlist, selected from submissions published in English in the UK over the past year, range from biography and ancient history to espionage, true crime and international reportage. The prize is widely regarded as the UK’s most prestigious award for nonfiction. “Chairing this prize is like being part of a very well-informed and opinionated book group,” said lead judge Kirsty Lang. “Whittling our choices down to 13 books led to some forthright discussion, but we got there in the end and are very proud of our longlist.” Biography is a major theme of this year’s list. In Baldwin: A Love Story, the first major study of James Baldwin in 30 years, Nicholas Boggs examines Baldwin’s relationships and their influence on his writing, drawing on previously unseen material and interviews. The life of another literary figure is explored in The Great Dictator by Matthew Sweet. Sweet’s account of the romance novelist Barbara Cartland’s career is set against the backdrop of the changing sexual and social politics of her era. Meanwhile, Andrea Wulf’s The Traveller examines the largely forgotten 18th-century explorer George Forster, who joined Captain Cook’s second voyage around the world as a teenager. Contemporary conflicts also loom large. In Days of Love and Rage, Anand Gopal reports from Manbij, Syria, during the revolution, telling the stories of people who helped overthrow a dictatorship. The Bookseller of Kabul author Åsne Seierstad offers an account of contemporary Russia in Never Say War; while Ian Buruma’s Stay Alive: Berlin, 1939–1945 examines how ordinary people navigated life under the Nazi regime. Ancient history is represented by Edmund Richardson’s Alexander: God, King, Man, a portrait of Alexander the Great. In The Nord Stream Conspiracy the Wall Street Journal political correspondent Bojan Pancevski probes the sabotage of North Sea gas pipelines. While Murder in Paris ’68 by Edward Chisholm revisits one of French cinema’s most notorious scandals: the murder of actor Alain Delon’s bodyguard, Stefan Marković. Completing this year’s longlist, Jane Rogoyska’s Hotel Exile tells the wartime story of the Hôtel Lutetia in Paris which was transformed from a gathering place for refugee artists, activists and intellectuals into the headquarters of Nazi intelligence. The longlist was selected by Lang, Waterstones’s head of books Bea Carvalho, writer and cultural historian Tiffany Jenkins, Spectator literary editor Sam Leith, editor and reporter Ravi Mattu and novelist Elif Shafak. The prize, established as the Samuel Johnson prize in 1999, has been sponsored by Edinburgh-based investment management firm Baillie Gifford since 2016. The company has faced criticism in recent years over its investments in fossil fuels and companies with links to Israel. In 2024, campaign group Fossil Free Books organised boycotts of literary festivals sponsored by the firm, resulting in Baillie Gifford ending its partnerships with nine festivals. The winner will receive £50,000, with the shortlist of six announced on 1 October and the winner on 4 November. Last year’s prize was won by Australian writer Helen Garner for How to End a Story: Collected Diaries. Browse all the books on the Baillie Gifford 2025 longlist at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.
chineseTitle: 间谍活动、真实犯罪和战争：Baillie Gifford 长名单揭晓
chineseSummary: 帕特里克·拉登·基夫 (Patrick Radden Keefe)、本·麦金泰尔 (Ben Macintyre) 和《卫报》的夏洛特·希金斯 (Charlotte Higgins) 是入选非小说类小说奖的 13 名作家之一
chineseContent: 《卫报》首席文化作家夏洛特·希金斯 (Charlotte Higgins) 与美国调查记者帕特里克·拉登·基夫 (Patrick Radden Keefe) 和畅销书历史学家本·麦金泰尔 (Ben Macintyre) 一起进入了今年的贝利·吉福德奖长名单。希金斯的书《乌克兰的教训：战争时期的艺术》借鉴了多次前往乌克兰的报道，探讨了文化在乌克兰抵抗俄罗斯入侵中的作用。基夫于 2021 年凭借《痛苦帝国》获奖，凭借《伦敦坠落》再次入围，该片讲述了青少年扎克·布雷特勒 (Zac Brettler) 的故事，他冒充俄罗斯富有寡头的儿子，从伦敦豪华公寓坠落。麦金太尔的《红木：冷战时期最非凡间谍不为人知的故事》讲述了军情六处在革命的德黑兰培养的克格勃双重间谍的故事。入围名单上的 13 本书是从去年在英国出版的英文版书籍中选出的，内容涵盖传记、古代历史、间谍、真实犯罪和国际报告文学等。该奖项被广泛认为是英国最负盛名的非小说类奖项。 “担任该奖项的主席就像是一个消息灵通、固执己见的图书小组的一员，”首席评委柯斯蒂·朗 (Kirsty Lang) 说道。 “将我们的选择减少到 13 本书引发了一​​些直率的讨论，但我们最终还是做到了这一点，并对我们的长名单感到非常自豪。”传记是今年榜单的一大主题。在《鲍德温：一个爱情故事》中，尼古拉斯·博格斯利用前所未见的材料和采访，探讨了鲍德温的人际关系及其对他写作的影响，这是 30 年来首部对詹姆斯·鲍德温的重大研究。马修·斯威特在《大独裁者》中探讨了另一位文学人物的生活。斯威特对浪漫小说家芭芭拉·卡特兰职业生涯的描述是以性别和性别不断变化的背景为背景的。
